_comment: Tier B source specification, executed CLIENT-SIDE by OpenASN clients (the Ruby gem's update job). These sources have terms that permit fetching from the original authority but NOT third-party redistribution, or they change too fast for a nightly artifact (Tor exits) - so OpenASN publishes the recipe, never the data (the fetch-is-not-redistribute rule; see README Legal design). Clients: send a descriptive User-Agent, honor cadence_hours, keep stale data on failure, and skip source ids or parser ids you don't recognize (forward compatibility).

sources.notes: ~280k rows; MUST aggregate (merges to a few tens of thousands of ranges). Apple posts this list publicly for recognition and says to treat Private Relay like carrier-grade NAT: recognize, don't block (https://developer.apple.com/icloud/prepare-your-network-for-icloud-private-relay/). Egress IPs live inside Cloudflare/Akamai space - relay MUST outrank hosting in client precedence.
Official Tor Project bulk exit list. Do NOT substitute dan.me.uk (bans fetchers for 30 min on over-fetch).
Official. Parse prefixes[].ip_prefix and ipv6_prefixes[].ipv6_prefix.
Customer ranges. goog.json (Google-owned infra) is deliberately not fetched: as-metadata already categorizes Google ASNs as hosting.
The actual ServiceTags_Public_YYYYMMDD.json URL rotates weekly behind the download page; clients must scrape the page for the current link and keep stale data when the scrape breaks.
Official OCI ranges: regions[].cidrs[].cidr.
RFC 8805-style geofeed CSV; first column is the CIDR.
RFC 8805 geofeed.
RFC 8805 geofeed (Constant = Vultr).

CONTEXT FLAG ONLY - never map to a blocking verdict. WARP and iCloud Private Relay egress live inside these ranges (that's why X4B excludes them from its dc list). Docs: https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/concepts/cloudflare-ip-addresses/

GitHub's own published address list, documented for allowlisting at https://docs.github.com/en/rest/meta/meta. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 7624 CIDRs across actions/actions_macos/codespaces/copilot/hooks/web/api/git/packages/pages/importer/github_enterprise_importer -> 2101 v4 + 648 v6 merged ranges. Parser takes every CIDR-shaped entry in every top-level array and ignores ssh_keys / commit_signing_keys / domains, so new service groups need no parser change. GitHub Actions egress dominates the file; this is the single best answer to 'is this hosting IP a CI runner?'. Off by default because the unauthenticated endpoint is rate-limited to 60 requests/hour per IP and the ranges are already inside AWS/Azure space that the cloud recipes cover - the value added is the ATTRIBUTION, not new coverage.

Atlassian publishes its cloud product ranges for firewall allowlisting: https://support.atlassian.com/organization-administration/docs/ip-addresses-and-domains-for-atlassian-cloud-products/. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, items[].cidr, 166 CIDRs -> 68 v4 + 8 v6 merged ranges. Covers both directions (ingress + egress); the egress rows are what a site sees when Jira/Confluence/Bitbucket webhooks and Connect apps call out.

Googlebot. Google publishes this list so sites can verify a crawler really is Googlebot: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/verifying-googlebot . Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 317 prefixes (170 v4 + 147 v6) - the only crawler operator in this set that publishes IPv6. NOTE the URL moved: the legacy /search/apis/ipranges/googlebot.json path still answers but the docs now point at /crawling/ipranges/common-crawlers.json (byte-identical content). 23 of the 317 prefixes are the geo-crawl /28s carved out of GCP space that OpenASN's gcp recipe also claims - which is exactly why crawler attribution is read from the `role` index instead of the maps_to ladder.

Google's special-case crawlers (AdsBot, AdSense, Google-Safety abuse crawler). Same publication and verification doc as Googlebot. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 272 prefixes (136 v4 + 136 v6); 0 of 272 fall inside GCP cloud.json and all 272 are inside goog.json, i.e. pure Google infrastructure. rDNS mask rate-limited-proxy-*.google.com.

Google fetchers that run because a PERSON asked (Site Verifier, Feedfetcher, Read Aloud, Google Pinpoint), from Google-owned IPs. role=verified_fetcher, not verified_crawler: a human is waiting on the response and Google documents that these do not follow all robots.txt directives, so throttling them throttles a user. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 496 prefixes (248 v4 + 248 v6); 496/496 inside goog.json and 0/496 inside GCP cloud.json.

Google-Agent: the fetcher behind Google's agentic products, which Google's docs tie to Web Bot Auth (agent.bot.goog). Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 20 prefixes (12 v4 + 8 v6). 4 of the 20 (136.121.16.0/24, 136.121.24.0/21, 136.121.40.0/21, 136.122.0.0/16) are NOT in goog.json, so goog.json is not a substitute for this feed. Smallest and most future-relevant list in the set.

DELIBERATELY CARRIES NO role. These IPs resolve to *.gae.googleusercontent.com: SHARED App Engine egress used by arbitrary third-party customer code, not by Google's own fetchers. Attributing this range to Google as a verified fetcher would be a false statement about whoever's app is actually calling. Kept as an opt-in hosting source only. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 1058 prefixes (529 v4 + 529 v6).

Google-announced infrastructure, the coarse superset behind goog.json. NOT a crawler list and deliberately given no role: it contains 8.8.8.0/24 (Public DNS) and aggregated /15-/12 blocks, and it is a superset of GCP customer space that the gcp recipe already covers precisely. Useful mainly as a negative check ('this is not Google at all'). Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 145 prefixes (130 v4 + 15 v6); note the extra top-level syncToken key the crawler files lack. This is the goog.json-vs-cloud.json question the gcp recipe's note left open: cloud.json stays the default, goog.json stays opt-in.

Bingbot's first-party list. Off by default for an evidence reason, not a technical one: no retrievable Microsoft sentence establishes the file is published for recognition (Bing Webmaster help is a JS SPA that serves no prose to a plain fetcher, and the only first-party text found says the opposite - a Dec 2018 Bing blog post: 'Since Bing does not release the list of IPs'). Promote to enabled_default once someone quotes a current Microsoft page. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 28 prefixes, IPv4 only. Two traps: in-body creationTime is frozen at 2024-01-03 while HTTP Last-Modified is 2026-08-27 (use the header), and 27 of the 28 prefixes are inside Azure ServiceTags.

OpenAI's training crawler, published at https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots for allowlisting. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 21 prefixes, IPv4 only. Publishers routinely block GPTBot while allowing OAI-SearchBot, so the three OpenAI feeds are separate sources on purpose. Every OpenAI prefix sits inside Azure ServiceTags - attribution comes from the role index, not the hosting ladder.

ChatGPT-User: a live person asked ChatGPT to open this page. role=verified_fetcher because a human is waiting; blocking it is blocking a user, not a bot. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 207 prefixes, IPv4 only, creationTime one day old - by far the fastest-churning feed in the set, hence cadence_hours 6. Served MINIFIED on one line while OpenAI's other files are pretty-printed: parse as JSON, never line-wise.
OAI-SearchBot indexes pages for ChatGPT search results. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 35 prefixes, IPv4 only.

OAI-AdsBot validates ad landing pages. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 2 prefixes (130.131.229.128/25, 20.168.90.128/25). Trivially small; included because the cost is one conditional GET and the attribution is otherwise unavailable.

Anthropic's COMBINED crawler list: ClaudeBot, Claude-User and Claude-SearchBot share one file with no per-bot labels, so they cannot be separated by IP and are attributed together as 'claudebot'. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 26 prefixes, IPv4 only; 20 of the 26 are single-host /32s. www.anthropic.com/claudebot.json does NOT exist (404 returning a Next.js error page that is easily mistaken for a feed). Freshness must come from the in-body creationTime, which is Z-suffixed here and naive-microsecond everywhere else; no Last-Modified header is served. The feed spans AWS, GCP and Azure at once - only 216.73.216.0/22 (RDAP netname AWS-ANTHROPIC) is durably registered to Anthropic, so never pin the rest.

Applebot, published under Apple's 'Identifying Applebot' documentation. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 33 prefixes, IPv4 only, all inside 17.0.0.0/8. THE APPLEBOT-vs-PRIVATE-RELAY COLLISION WAS MEASURED AND IS CLEARED: Apple's own relay egress list (287,841 rows) contains no prefix inside 17/8 at all - Private Relay egresses from partner CDN space. Match the 33 published CIDRs and never 17.0.0.0/8, which would sweep in Apple corporate and consumer devices.

Common Crawl's CCBot, the crawler behind the dataset most open LLM training corpora derive from. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 5 prefixes (4 v4 + 1 v6) which the file's own notes field calls dedicated ranges - the cleanest list in the set. Its notes also recommend FCrDNS as a second check for IPv4.

DuckDuckBot. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 486 IPv4 /32s, creationTime 4 days old - the freshest feed in the set. duckassistbot.json is deliberately NOT a second source: it is BYTE-IDENTICAL to this file (same 32,101 bytes, same MD5, same creationTime), so DuckDuckGo publishes one shared egress pool and adding it would imply an IP-level search-vs-AI distinction the operator does not actually make.

PerplexityBot. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 8 prefixes = 18 addresses; values are NOT all /32 (18.97.1.228/30, 18.97.9.96/29), so honour the published prefix length. COVERAGE CAVEAT worth knowing: Cloudflare reported in August 2025 that Perplexity also crawled from undeclared IPs outside this list using a generic browser user agent. That makes the list incomplete, which is a false NEGATIVE - the safe direction - but it means absence from this list is not evidence a request is not Perplexity.

Perplexity-User: fetches triggered by a person's question. role=verified_fetcher; Perplexity documents that it generally ignores robots.txt for these because a user is waiting. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 4 prefixes = 14 addresses, mixed /32 /30 /29.

Amazonbot. Off by default for cost and staleness, not doubt: the list is a ~490 KB HTML documentation page wrapping ~25 KB of JSON, and its creationTime was 2026-04-30 when fetched on 2026-09-05. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 524 bare IPv4 addresses (no /32 suffix - the parser appends it). All 524 are single AWS EC2 hosts, so a stale entry can only mis-ATTRIBUTE, never mislabel a human; but EC2 addresses are recycled, which is the real reason to keep this opt-in.

Amzn-SearchBot. Same HTML-wrapped publication as amazonbot but with AWS's ip_prefix key and the /32 already present - the parser normalises both. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 512 IPv4 /32s, creationTime 2025-11-21 (roughly 9.5 months stale).

Amzn-User, Amazon's user-triggered fetcher (role=verified_fetcher: a person asked). Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 1023 bare IPv4 addresses, creationTime 2025-11-04 - the stalest and largest of the three Amazon lists, so the EC2 address-recycling risk is highest here. Opt-in.

CONTEXT FLAG ONLY, exactly like cloudflare_ranges - never a blocking verdict, and deliberately NOT hosting. Fastly's own API reference frames this list as 'firewall rules for connections from Fastly to your origin' (https://www.fastly.com/documentation/reference/api/utils/public-ip-list), i.e. these are the SOURCE addresses of proxied end-user requests. Any Fastly-fronted site that ignores Fastly-Client-IP / X-Forwarded-For sees every real human visitor arriving from these 21 prefixes; 151.101.0.0/16 alone fronts a large slice of the top web. Labelling that hosting would stamp a machine label on real people at web scale. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 402 bytes, 19 v4 + 2 v6. Nuance for the flag's consumers: Fastly Compute customer code egresses from this same anycast space, so a minority of traffic here really is customer-programmable automation - a reason to annotate the flag, not to reclassify the block.

Huawei Cloud's RFC 8805 geofeed. Found via RFC 9632 whois discovery, not documentation: the geofeed: attribute is published on five Huawei Cloud APNIC objects, which is what makes this a first-party publication rather than a scrape. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 33 KB, 927 rows -> 868 v4 + 59 v6. Uses the existing geofeed_csv parser unchanged.

Scaleway (Online SAS / Iliad) never built an ip-ranges endpoint; the authoritative statement is a documentation page, and scaleway.com serves it as raw markdown at the .md URL above (200, text/markdown, 2373 bytes, verified live 2026-09-12 - byte-identical to the MDX in Scaleway's own docs repo, so we cite the first-party domain and depend on nobody else). Section '## IP ranges used by Scaleway' -> 12 v4 + 1 v6, merged to 11 v4 + 1 v6. The parser STOPS at the next H2 on purpose: the following section lists bare DNS/NTP resolver addresses in the same bullet style and is not prefix data. FP note: 78.232.0.0/16 sits inside historically-Free-SAS residential space but RIPE gives netname SCALEWAY / org Scaleway / ASSIGNED PA, so labelling it hosting corrects stale geo data rather than mislabelling people. Opt-in because Scaleway's ASNs (AS12876, AS51207) already carry hosting from the core artifact; this recipe buys range-level precision and provider attribution.

IBM Cloud Classic (ex-SoftLayer) front-end, load-balancer and legacy public ranges. IBM's docs platform serves any page as markdown with &format=markdown (documented at https://cloud.ibm.com/docs/llms.txt); the human URL is a JS-rendered SPA containing ZERO CIDRs, so the markdown export is the only machine path. Verified live 2026-09-12: 200, text/markdown, 37832 bytes, last-updated 2026-06-09. DANGER, and the reason the parser is section-filtered AND RFC1918-guarded: 509 of the document's 759 CIDRs are private space (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) belonging to the back-end, service and SSL VPN networks - ingesting the page whole would label every home and office LAN on earth as IBM hosting. The parser reads only 'Front-end (public) network', 'Load balancer IPs' and 'Legacy networks' -> 90 tokens, 60 merged v4, 0 v6. Deliberately EXCLUDED: 'Red Hat Enterprise Linux server requirements' and 'Windows virtual server instance requirements', which list endpoints an IBM customer must reach (Red Hat, Microsoft WSUS) and are not IBM address space. Coverage is thin by design - this is IBM's own infrastructure subnets, not customer allocations, and IBM Cloud VPC (the modern platform) is not covered anywhere. Do NOT substitute https://ibm.biz/cidr-calculator: IBM itself disclaims it as a community tool.

OVHcloud shared web hosting: 24 clusters, each publishing per-country inbound VIPs plus a shared-CDN address and - the valuable part - ONE outgoing NAT gateway. Every PHP script on a cluster egresses from that single address, so traffic a site receives from e.g. 91.134.248.230 is by construction server-side automation, never a human browsing. OVH invites machine consumption in the page body ('this page is available as Markdown at ...clusters-and-shared-hosting-ip.md'); verified live 2026-09-12: 200, text/markdown, 37840 bytes, lastUpdated 2026-07-21, 24/24 gateways captured, 479 host routes -> 259 v4 + 66 v6. FETCH GOTCHA: the same URL WITH a trailing slash returns a 404 page. CONSUMER WARNING: the gateways are high-tenancy shared egress - thousands of tenant sites behind one address - so per-IP reputation decisions punish everyone on the cluster at once; classify, do not block. SCOPE: shared hosting only. OVH's bare metal, VPS and Public Cloud estates - the overwhelming majority of OVH space and of OVH-sourced abuse - are published nowhere: no ip-ranges endpoint exists, geofeed.ovh.net does not resolve, and OVH's RIPE objects carry no geofeed: attribute (checked 2026-09-05).

MistralAI-User: fetches triggered by a person's question to Le Chat. role=verified_fetcher. Found via docs.mistral.ai/robots - the documented /crawlers paths 404. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 279 bytes, 4 IPv4 /32s in Azure space.
MistralAI-Index: indexing crawler, documented as indexing-only with no AI training use. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 176 bytes, 2 IPv4 /32s.

AhrefsBot, the SEO crawler. Public and unauthenticated despite the api. hostname; documented at https://ahrefs.com/robot (note ahrefs.com/robot/crawler-ips 404s). Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 3350 bytes, 81 prefixes, IPv4 only, same {prefixes:[{ipv4Prefix}]} envelope as the Google-shaped feeds but with NO creationTime key. Ahrefs also publishes an individual-IP endpoint (/crawler-ips, 10,350 entries, 403 KB) covering the SAME space at 120x the bytes - deliberately not used. Opt-in: a commercial SEO crawler is lower value to most consumers than the search and AI operators.

Exit IPs scraped from ProtonVPN's own API by tn3w/ProtonVPN-IPs (LICENSE verified Apache-2.0, default branch master). Proton's official API now requires app headers/session auth for anonymous callers (verified 2026-07-05), so this licensed feed remains the clean default until Proton publishes a stable public endpoint.

First-party public relay API used by Mullvad's server list (https://mullvad.net/en/servers). Parser keeps active exact relay IPs only (ipv4_addr_in/ipv6_addr_in); do NOT widen to /24. Mozilla VPN / Firefox VPN use Mullvad infrastructure (https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/products/vpn/resource-center/vpn-servers-around-the-world/), but the egress IP cannot distinguish Mozilla users from direct Mullvad users, so provider attribution stays 'Mullvad'.
First-party IVPN server status JSON linked from/supporting https://www.ivpn.net/en/status/. Parser collects exact WireGuard hosts[].host and OpenVPN ip_addresses[].
First-party PIA client server list. Body is JSON on the first line followed by a detached signature; parser reads region server IPs for WireGuard/OpenVPN/IKEv2/meta groups and skips offline regions.

First-party public status API (AirVPN forum confirms it lists all servers and entry IP addresses: https://airvpn.org/forums/topic/74903-servers-ips-list/). Parser collects ip_v4_in*/ip_v6_in* exact entry IPs; deprecated ip_entry fields are intentionally ignored.

Windscribe's first-party mobile client server list: exact node/ping IPs. Live 2026-09-12: 200, application/json, 305 KB, 1076 tokens -> 395 v4 ranges. THE 403 IS GONE. On 2026-09-05 every Windscribe path answered with a Cloudflare challenge interstitial and this recipe was demoted to opt-in; on 2026-09-12 a plain unauthenticated GET with a descriptive User-Agent returns 200 from two independent checks (the manifest health check and a separate live probe). Restored to enabled_default. If it 403s again, that is a CDN policy flap and not a takedown - keep_stale means an overlay fetched earlier keeps classifying, and Tier B runs on the end user's own network, so a block seen here may not exist there. Shape unchanged: data[] locations -> groups[] -> nodes[]; union groups[].ping_ip with nodes[].ip/.ip2/.ip3 (ip2 and ip3 are optional). A flatter fallback with the same node IPs lives at https://assets.windscribe.com/serverlist/openvpn/1/0 (200, 229 KB, no groups[], no ping_ip).

Opt-in: first-party NordVPN API returns exact station/ips[].ip.ip values. v2 is still large (~10MB live on 2026-07-05), so keep behind config.tier_b[:vpn_heavy]. Official server list docs: https://support.nordvpn.com/hc/en-us/articles/19383127694225-Where-can-I-find-the-NordVPN-server-list

First-party PrivadoVPN app server export discovered via public client tooling and verified live 2026-07-05. Parser reads servers[].ip exact exit/server IPs and ignores hostname/load/location metadata.

First-party LEAP/Bitmask provider API for RiseupVPN. OONI's RiseupVPN test documents that this provider API returns VPN gateway IP addresses and capabilities (https://github.com/ooni/spec/blob/master/nettests/ts-026-riseupvpn.md). Parser reads gateways[].ip_address exact IPs.

First-party WLVPN/IPVanish white-label server API. WLVPN's site says it is a white-label VPN solution powered by IPVanish and part of VIPRE Security Group, a Ziff Davis company (https://wlvpn.com/about-wlvpn/). Parser keeps only server elements with visible=1/status=1 and reads exact ip attributes. Provider attribution is intentionally WLVPN backend infrastructure, not a reseller brand such as Spaceship/FastVPN or Namecheap FastVPN.

First-party WorldVPN public server table. The page publishes exact IPs beside *.ocservvpn.com hostnames and says all listed servers support multiple VPN protocols, with OpenVPN profiles linked per row. Parser reads only table rows whose host cell is *.ocservvpn.com and emits the exact IP cell; no DNS expansion or whole-page IP scraping.

OVPN's first-party client bootstrap API: the whole fleet in ONE request. REPLACES ovpn_status_servers, which fetched thirty-two status-page endpoints (one per datacenter) for the same answer - verified 2026-09-12 that both yield 96 exact IPs -> 34 merged v4 ranges, so this is a 32x reduction in requests against a provider's own infrastructure at zero data cost. Live 2026-09-12: 200, application/json, 36177 bytes, 32 datacenters. Shape: {success, datacenters:[{slug, city, ping_address, pools:[hostname], servers:[{ip, ptr, online, load, public_key, wireguard_ports}]}], shadowsocks:{...}}. The parser takes datacenters[].ping_address and datacenters[].servers[].ip and DELIBERATELY DOES NOT filter on `online` - a server briefly down is still OVPN egress, and filtering would make the overlay flap. It also reads nothing outside `datacenters`: the sibling `shadowsocks` object carries a shared credential, so this response body must never be logged. No IPv6 anywhere in the fleet. The old recipe's id is retired rather than reused because its name described a status page that is no longer the source; overlays keyed to the old id are simply never loaded once the id leaves the feature map.

First-party JSON endpoint called by Anonine's public Network page Gatsby bundle (serverStatusUrl() -> /www/server-status). Parser reads exact primary_ip values and servers[].ips arrays. The endpoint also includes host aliases, but OpenASN uses exact IPs here so this can stay in the default exact-IP provider set.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: AzireVPN's official API docs publish the unauthenticated GET /v3/locations endpoint and describe the pool field as the hostname pool with IPs available for the location (https://www.azirevpn.com/docs/api/locations). Clients resolve those pool hostnames locally, so results stay behind config.tier_b[:vpn_dns]. AzireVPN's current site/legal footer redirects to Malwarebytes legal pages and says (c) 2012-2026 Malwarebytes.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: VPN.AC's official VPN Nodes Status page publishes exact *.vpn.ac hostnames in the status table, and its official /ovpn/ directory publishes matching OpenVPN config bundles. Clients resolve the hostnames locally because the page publishes hostnames, not raw IPs.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: Trust.Zone's first-party Zones & Servers page publishes exact *.trust.zone zone hostnames. Manual OpenVPN setup pages keep the downloadable .ovpn files hidden behind login, so this source intentionally uses only the public server page and local DNS resolution.

Cryptostorm's first-party OpenVPN config archive, served from an open directory index on the provider's own domain. Live 2026-09-12: 200, application/zip, 485048 bytes, 92 .ovpn members at the archive root -> 138 unique exact hostnames, ZERO literal IPs, which is why this is a DNS-expanded opt-in (vpn_dns) rather than an exact-IP recipe. No new parser needed: the existing ovpn_zip_remote_hosts reads it unchanged (its /\Aremote\s+([^\s]+)/ pattern is not anchored on the two-token form, so Cryptostorm's three-token 'remote <host> <port> <proto>' lines parse correctly - confirmed by running it against the live archive). Each config carries THREE remote lines, one per mirror zone (cstorm.is / cstorm.net / cryptostorm.pw), and all three are emitted: dedupe on the full FQDN, not the leftmost label, or 138 collapses to 46. 'balancer.<zone>' is a round-robin name whose answers churn, which is normal for this class of source.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party Surfshark cluster API publishes connectionName hostnames, not raw IPs. Clients resolve those hostnames locally at update time, so results can vary by DNS vantage and should stay behind config.tier_b[:vpn_dns].
Opt-in DNS-expanded Surfshark static-IP cluster hostnames. See surfshark_generic for the DNS-vantage caveat.
Opt-in DNS-expanded Surfshark obfuscated cluster hostnames. The double-hop cluster endpoint returned an empty list live on 2026-07-05, so it is intentionally not included.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party IPVanish OpenVPN config archive linked by router/client documentation. Archive contains remote hostnames (thousands), so clients resolve locally and keep this behind config.tier_b[:vpn_dns].
Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party PrivateVPN OpenVPN TUN archive. Parser extracts remote hostnames and clients resolve them locally.
Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party/PureVPN router OpenVPN archive used by client tooling. Parser extracts remote hostnames and clients resolve them locally.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party TorGuard TCP OpenVPN archive. The earlier servers.json endpoint hit a bot challenge, but these public config archives fetched cleanly live on 2026-07-05. 2026-09-05 re-check: 403 with Cloudflare 'error code: 1005', which is an ASN-level ban of the network the check ran from - NOT evidence the archive is gone. Left enabled-capable on purpose: Tier B is executed by the end user's own server, and keep_stale absorbs a 403 from a banned vantage.
Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party TorGuard UDP OpenVPN archive. Usually overlaps TCP, but keeping both avoids silent protocol-specific omissions.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party FastestVPN support page AJAX endpoint used by https://support.fastestvpn.com/vpn-servers/. Parser reads hostnames from the returned HTML table; clients resolve locally.
Opt-in DNS-expanded source: first-party FastestVPN UDP host table. Kept separate from TCP to avoid silent protocol-specific omissions.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: TunnelBear's first-party Linux setup article links this public OpenVPN ZIP. Parser extracts exact remote hostnames, including provider files suffixed .ovpn.txt; clients resolve them locally.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: StrongVPN/StrongTech first-party locations page publishes exact vpn-*.reliablehosting.com server hostnames. Clients resolve locally because the page publishes hostnames, not raw IPs; live smoke on 2026-07-05 saw many stale DNS names, so keep behind config.tier_b[:vpn_dns].

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: VyprVPN's first-party support article links this public OpenVPN ZIP (filename VyprVPN_OpenVPN_2026-03-06.zip; fetched 2026-07-05 with Last-Modified 2026-06-18). Parser extracts exact *.vyprvpn.com remote hostnames; clients resolve them locally. Some embedded cert metadata still names Golden Frog, which is legacy branding for the current Certida-operated service.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: Giganews first-party support page publishes exact *.vpn.giganews.com hostnames for VyprVPN bundled with Giganews accounts and says IP addresses are subject to change, so clients resolve hostnames locally.

Opt-in DNS-expanded source: SlickVPN's first-party locations page says these are active VPN servers and links public 2025 OpenVPN configs under members.newsdemon.com. Parser extracts only the config-linked visible gw*.slickvpn.com hostnames from that page. In the 2026-07-05 smoke the Amsterdam page label resolved while the linked config's remote did not, so the active server page is the source of record and config files are corroboration only.

Opt-in public/free VPN source: VPNBook publishes current OpenVPN server hostnames on this page; clients resolve them locally. Keep behind config.tier_b[:public_relays] because free public VPN endpoints are high-churn.

Opt-in public/free VPN source: FreeVPN.us (Roosterkid) publishes a live status table with data-type/data-host attributes. Parser keeps only OpenVPN, WireGuard, and PPTP/L2TP VPN rows and intentionally excludes SSH Tunnel and V2Ray rows from the VPN overlay. Clients resolve *.vpnv.cc locally; keep behind config.tier_b[:public_relays] because free public endpoints are high-churn.

Opt-in: official VPN Gate Academic Experiment public relay API. These are volunteer relays, often residential/ISP IPs while actively serving VPN traffic; exact current hits are valuable but high-churn, so keep behind config.tier_b[:public_relays]. Parser reads the CSV IP column only and ignores embedded OpenVPN configs.

Cloud Enforcement Node Ranges, published for allowlisting (verified live 2026-07-04: nested JSON, collect every 'range' value, both v4 and v6; re-verified 2026-09-05: 200, 935 ranges -> 673 networks). Off by default: the ASN-level enterprise_gateway overrides already cover Zscaler; enable for finer range-level coverage. Zscaler serves several named clouds at the same API path; measured 2026-09-05, zscalerone/two/three/zscloud/zscalerbeta are 99%+ duplicates of this file (36 new networks across all five), so only the separately-addressed government cloud below is worth a second fetch.

Zscaler's FedRAMP-authorized US government cloud, same CENR API and JSON shape as zscaler.net. Verified live 2026-09-05: 200, 30 ranges -> 6 v4 + 7 v6 networks, ALL 30 absent from zscaler.net - this is the one sibling cloud that is not a duplicate. Behind these IPs are US federal/state agency employees browsing from the office, so the enterprise_gateway (likely-human) semantics are exactly right.

Cisco Secure Service Edge egress - ONE feed covers BOTH Umbrella SWG and Cisco Secure Access ('The feed includes deployed egress prefixes for Cisco SSE products, including Secure Access and Umbrella'), so no per-product recipe is needed. It is an RFC 8805 geofeed, and Cisco self-publishes the URL in RIR whois as an RFC 9092 geofeed reference (whois 151.186.1.1 -> 'remarks: Geofeed https://geofeed.network.strln.net/'), which is what makes unattended machine consumption the documented purpose rather than a scrape. Host provenance verified: strln.net whois registrant 'OpenDNS Hostmaster', 170 W. Tasman Drive San Jose (Cisco HQ), NS AUTH1/2/3.OPENDNS.COM. Verified live 2026-09-12: 200, 56539 bytes, Last-Modified same day, 1865 records -> 86 v4 + 65 v6 merged ranges. Content-Type is binary/octet-stream, NOT text/csv - do not content-type-sniff. Uses geofeed_csv_no_widen rather than geofeed_csv because 142 IPv6 rows carry a bogus /32 on a single host address ('2603:5004:e0:107::135b/32'); masking those would claim all of 2603:5004::/32 on the evidence of a pinhole. THE RESOLVERS ARE CORRECTLY ABSENT: 208.67.222.0/24 and 208.67.220.0/24 (the OpenDNS public resolvers) are NOT in the feed, so using it verbatim does not walk into the D-ENRICH-1 trap of labelling a public DNS resolver enterprise_gateway. Coverage caveat: the feed lists DEPLOYED prefixes only, so documented-but-unused allowlist space lags - Cisco documents 9.240.0.0/15 as shared SWG egress and there is not one 9.x record in the feed. That biases us toward false negatives, which is the preference.

Cato Networks SASE PoP egress. Cato publishes the list expressly for third-party allowlisting: 'We recommend that you add the IP ranges owned by Cato Networks to the relevant ACL ... to allow traffic to the Cato Cloud'. knowledge.catonetworks.com serves it unauthenticated (robots.txt is 'User-agent: * / Allow: /' with no Disallow); verified live 2026-09-12: 200, text/html, 1,644,504 bytes -> 43 CIDRs -> 40 v4 ranges, 0 v6. USE THIS HOST ONLY: www.catonetworks.com sits behind Imperva/Incapsula and answers automated clients with a 949-byte incident page, and support.catonetworks.com (Zendesk) 403s. The CSV attachment on cdn.document360.io is nicer but its URL carries a 15-minute Azure SAS token and 404s without it, so it cannot be a manifest URL. Cato's ASN is AS13150 (RIPE RDAP: handle AS13150, name CATON, org ORG-CNL17-RIPE 'CATO NETWORKS LTD'; RPKI ROAs to AS13150 for 45.62.176.0/20, 199.27.32.0/19, 216.205.112.0/20). NOT AS37927, which is NOMURATRADE in JPNIC. An AS13150 override would be cheaper, but this list also captures leased China / Casablanca / Singapore / Seoul space that AS13150 does not announce - and that leased space is also the recipe's one real risk: if Cato hands a Chinese carrier range back, it reverts to ordinary ISP allocation and we would carry a stale enterprise_gateway label for up to a week. Acceptable because enterprise_gateway is a likely-human, never-blocking verdict. Spot-verified in ARIN RDAP 2026-09-12: 149.20.192.0 -> CATO-NETWORKSINC, 150.195.192.0 and 216.194.96.0 -> CN-238, 45.62.176.0 -> CATO-NETWORKS-INC, all registrant 'Cato Networks Inc'.

SEMANTIC WARNING (from their own README): includes ASNs of providers 'permissive toward pentesting, DDoS, bot operations' - broader than VPN. Never map to :vpn; exposed only as a flag. Off by default. Interim IPv6 VPN-ish signal for those who opt in.
